betterCitation: Praxilla, Hymn to Adonis, fragment 747 PMG (Adonis) (trans. Richmond Lattimore, Greek Lyrics, 2nd edn, 1960, p. 49)
reason: Attacked at the point the verifier itself flagged, and it held. I reached Lattimore’s Greek Lyrics itself: Internet Archive item greek-lyrics-lattimore-richmond-alexander, whose title page reads GREEK LYRICS, Translated by Richmond Lattimore, SECOND EDITION, REVISED AND ENLARGED, THE UNIVERSITY OF CHICAGO PRESS, and whose copyright page reads Published 1955. Second Edition 1960. That is exactly the named edition. The Praxilla leaf, page numbered 49, prints the three lines in precisely the wording the verifier would ship, comma after the sunlight included, lower case at the second and third line heads, curly apostrophe in moon’s face, full stop after apples. Lattimore’s own headnote on that page says Adonis is the speaker of these lines, so the (Adonis) parenthetical is right. One correction to the EVIDENCE, not to the line: the University of Miami page the verifier called its primary witness does not in fact agree, it prints line one with no comma after the sunlight, so the claim that three citations agree on this wording is overstated; Tom Clark's posting does carry the comma, and the book settles it. The note must be rewritten before it ships, because it says no page of Greek Lyrics was sighted and one now has been, at p. 49. Everything else checks: shipped.js returns nothing shipped and nothing near, Praxilla at 0 of 3, not banned; source line 99 characters, leads with the name, no dash, no straight double quote; verse in the edition's own lineation with the slash marks; Poetry is the form of the work; a fifth-century BC lyric is in scope; nothing here needs a content warning; and it is squarely the August theme. The one loose joint, not enough to refute: 747 PMG is Page's numbering from Poetae Melici Graeci (1962) and Lattimore prints no fragment number at all, so the locator postdates the translation, but PMG 747 is the correct standard reference for this fragment and stands independently of who englished it.
